author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, a full generation has grown up without a personal memory of the day, learning about it through relatives, classrooms, online archives and the wars that followed.

Reuters collected accounts from people born around or after 2001 in the United States and other countries. Their experiences show how an event shifts from lived memory to history while continuing to influence ideas about national security, American power and public grief.

For some, the first explanation came from parents who described where they were. Others encountered the attacks through school lessons or images online. The nearly 3,000 deaths remain central to commemoration, but younger people also place the day within a longer story that includes military conflicts and changes in travel and surveillance.

The transition creates a challenge for educators and museums: preserve factual detail and individual experiences without assuming students remember the atmosphere of 2001. The 25th anniversary makes that task more visible as commemorations increasingly bring together witnesses, survivors and adults for whom September 11 has always been a historical event.
dek: Reuters gathered accounts from people too young to remember the attacks about how schools, families and later events shaped their understanding.
headline: A generation understands September 11 as history, not memory
